initial_requirements: Content delivery network providers need a software infrastructure that lets otherwise independent CDNs cooperate when demand exceeds local capacity. Providers should be able to discover potential peers, negotiate resource-sharing relationships and policies, replicate content, redirect user requests, and exchange load and accounting information. The arrangement should adapt to changing demand, protect information each provider chooses not to share, and support orderly expansion or termination.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What are the primary business goals this cross-CDN cooperation system must achieve, and how would you prioritize them when there is a tradeoff between capacity sharing, privacy of each provider’s information, and operational simplicity?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
The main business goal is to keep service available and fast when any one CDN is under pressure, without forcing providers to give up more control or data than they’re comfortable with. So first priority is protecting user experience and meeting demand through cooperation, then preserving each provider’s privacy and commercial boundaries, and after that keeping the operations simple enough that providers will actually use it.
If there’s a tradeoff, I’d usually favor limited, policy-driven sharing over broader access to internal information. In practice that means we want the system to share only what’s needed to make peering work, with privacy controls and clear opt-in policies, even if that makes the setup a bit more complex.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Who are the key stakeholders and participant roles that should be supported in this cross-CDN cooperation system, and what responsibilities or permissions does each role need?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
The key participants are the CDN providers themselves, since they own the capacity, policies, and content being shared. Each provider should be able to act through an administrator or operations team that can approve peering relationships, set sharing rules, choose what data to expose, and terminate arrangements when needed.
We also need a role for the system operators, if this is run as a shared platform or consortium service, to manage discovery, routing coordination, and possibly directory services without seeing everything each provider keeps private. On the technical side, automated components on each CDN need permissions to publish availability, receive assignments, exchange accounting data, and update content replication or request redirection decisions within the limits of the agreed policy.

turns.interviewer_utterance: Beyond the stakeholder roles we’ve identified, what are the essential end-to-end capabilities the system must provide from peering discovery through capacity sharing and request handling, and which of those capabilities are mandatory versus optional?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
At minimum, the system has to let a CDN find potential peers, establish a peering agreement, exchange the policy and capacity information needed to make the arrangement work, and then actually route or redirect traffic when one side needs help. It also needs basic accounting so everyone can see what was used and settle fairly afterward. Those are mandatory because without them the cooperation doesn’t really function.
Optional capabilities would be things like richer content replication strategies, automated optimization of peer selection, and more detailed analytics or forecasting. Those are useful, but if we had to cut scope, I’d keep the core discovery, negotiation, request handling, and accounting flows first.

turns.interviewer_utterance: What specific service-level objectives and overload thresholds should the system use to decide when a CDN needs peer assistance, and how should those targets be defined for availability, latency, or other performance measures?
turns.interviewee_utterance:
I’d expect the trigger to be based on each provider’s own service objectives, because the thresholds won’t be identical across CDNs. In practice, that usually means looking at sustained origin or edge utilization, request queueing, cache miss pressure, error rates, and latency against agreed targets, and then asking for peer help when those stay outside bounds for a defined period rather than on a brief spike.
For the actual numbers, I don’t think we should hardcode them globally. They should be configurable per provider and per service class, with different targets for availability and latency, because one CDN may care more about strict uptime while another may tolerate a little latency before offloading.

slots.name: project_goals
slots.value: Maintain service availability and performance when any one CDN is under pressure by enabling cooperation across CDNs; prioritize user experience and demand fulfillment first, then preserve each provider’s privacy and commercial boundaries, and finally keep operations simple enough for adoption. Favor limited, policy-driven sharing with privacy controls and clear opt-in policies over broad access to internal information.

slots.name: stakeholder_roles
slots.value: CDN providers as the primary participants; provider administrators or operations teams to approve peering, set sharing rules, control data exposure, and terminate arrangements; system operators or a consortium platform team to manage discovery, routing coordination, and directory services while respecting provider privacy; and automated CDN-side components that publish availability, receive assignments, exchange accounting data, and apply replication/redirection decisions within policy limits.

slots.name: functional_needs
slots.value: The system must support cross-CDN peering discovery, peering agreement establishment, exchange of policy and capacity information, request routing or redirection during overload, and basic accounting/settlement. Optional capabilities include richer content replication strategies, automated peer optimization, analytics, and forecasting.

slots.name: business_rules
slots.value: Peering should be policy-driven and opt-in. Providers can approve relationships, define sharing rules, choose what data is exposed, and terminate arrangements. Cooperation should use only the minimum information needed to make peering work, and accounting should support fair settlement after resource use.

slots.name: data_entities
slots.value: Policy and capacity information exchanged between peers; availability status published by each CDN; accounting and usage records for settlement. Potentially replicated content and routing/redirection assignments are also core data handled by the system.

slots.name: constraints
slots.value: The system must protect provider privacy and commercial boundaries by limiting shared information to what is necessary. System operators, if present, must manage coordination without exposing everything each provider keeps private. Sharing must occur under clear opt-in policies and agreed limits.

slots.name: quality_concerns
slots.value: Service availability and fast response under load are the highest quality concerns, followed by preserving privacy and provider control. Operational simplicity and adoption are also important, but secondary to performance and privacy.

slots.name: boundary_conditions
slots.value: The system must handle cases where a CDN is under pressure and needs help from peers, and support termination of peering arrangements when needed. If scope must be reduced, optional analytics, forecasting, and advanced replication should be excluded while preserving the core discovery, negotiation, request handling, and accounting functions.

slots.name: peer_discovery_and_matching
slots.value: A CDN must be able to find potential peers suitable for cooperation when local capacity is insufficient.

slots.name: resource_sharing_policy_management
slots.value: Providers must be able to negotiate and manage policy-driven resource-sharing relationships, including sharing rules, data exposure limits, and opt-in approval.

slots.name: content_replication_and_synchronization
slots.value: The system should support content replication, with richer replication strategies considered optional rather than mandatory.

slots.name: request_redirection_and_routing
slots.value: The system must route or redirect user traffic to cooperating peers when one CDN needs help handling demand.

slots.name: load_and_accounting_exchange
slots.value: Peers must exchange load, usage, and accounting information so each provider can see what was used and settle fairly afterward.

slots.name: peering_lifecycle_management
slots.value: The system must support establishing peering agreements and terminating arrangements when needed.

slots.name: policy_visibility_and_redaction_rules
slots.value: Only the minimum necessary information should be shared. Each provider should control what data is exposed, with privacy controls and limits that protect internal information and commercial boundaries.

slots.name: capacity_overload_triggers_and_thresholds
slots.value: Cooperation is triggered based on each provider’s own service objectives and overload conditions, using configurable per-provider and per-service-class thresholds rather than global hardcoded values. Triggers may consider sustained origin or edge utilization, request queueing, cache miss pressure, error rates, and latency staying outside agreed bounds for a defined period.

slots.name: routing_failover_and_fallback_behavior
slots.value: When a CDN cannot handle demand locally, traffic should be redirected to peers to preserve availability and performance; detailed fallback behavior was not specified.

slots.name: audit_logging_and_dispute_resolution
slots.value: Basic accounting is required to show what resources were used and support fair settlement afterward; explicit audit logging and dispute resolution requirements were not further defined.

slots.name: service_level_objectives_and_thresholds
slots.value: Service-level objectives and thresholds should be configurable per provider and per service class, with provider-specific targets for availability and latency rather than globally fixed values.
